newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt will resist pound appreciation.
newsitem.headline: Egypt will resist pound appreciation.

text.p: The Egyptian government will resist any tendency for the pound to appreciate against the dollar in the wake of the heavy capital inflows of the last few months, an economics minister said on Wednesday.
"The pound is not going to go up. We don't let it appreciate," Youssef Boutros-Ghali, minister of state for economic monitoring, told Reuters in an interview.
The pound has been steady at about 3.39 to 3.40 pounds to the dollar for more than two years, with the central bank buying surplus dollars or selling to cover any shortages.
Bankers say the central bank, acting mainly through the big four public-sector retail banks, has been buying dollars for several months to balance the foreign exchange market.
Boutros-Ghali said portfolio investments by foreigners had brought in between $600 million and $700 million this year and direct foreign investment had leaped to about $2 billion.
Most of the portfolio investment has been in the second half of the year, after the government accelerated its privatisation programme and the stock market started to rise.
The minister said the central bank's foreign reserves had risen to $18.9 billion, from $18.5 billion at the end of June.

He said the exchange rate policy was based on concern for Egyptian exporters, who have found it difficult to break into foreign markets. "Our exporters are used to working in a stable exchange rate environment. They would find it hard to handle an appreciating pound environment," he added.
Some foreign economists say the pound has become increasingly overvalued over the years because Egyptian inflation has been consistently higher than dollar inflation.
But Boutros-Ghali said the government continued to disagree. "It would be true if you extracted productivity gains through deregulation but those gains interrupt the link," he said.
"We estimate that productivity (in Egypt) is increasing between seven and 10 percent a year across the board. This is common in developing countries that deregulate," he said.
"Price competitiveness is not the issue (in Egypt's poor export performance). It's structural, it's the efficiency of marketing which has to be built from scratch," he added.
Egypt runs a massive trade deficit -- more than $9.2 billion in the financial year ended June 1996 -- but usually covers it through remittances from Egyptians abroad, tourism and other services.
Boutros-Ghali said the interest rate differential between the dollar and Egyptian pound was no longer the dominant factor in the pound's resilience to depreciation.
Pound deposits can earn more than 10 percent, against about five percent for dollar deposits in Egyptian banks. Four years ago the differential was more than 10 percentage points.
"The level of dollarisation (the proportion of deposits held in dollars) has recently fallen from 24 percent to 21 percent, although the (interest rate) differential had fallen," the minister said.
On the government's privatisation plans, Boutros-Ghali said sales through public subscription would continue despite the current preoccupation with the search for strategic investors.

The state said in September it would carry though an initial public offering (IPO) every week till the end of the year but in practice only two blocks of shares have come to the market through IPOs in the last seven weeks.
"We want to be sure the stock market is kept comfortably fed by issues. We're also looking to encourage the closed companies, the family concerns, to open up," the minister said.
But where public-sector companies need injections of technology, management or capital, the government would look for strategic investors, he added.
